summary: The note argues that small businesses are vital drivers of community development, supplying jobs, civic spirit, innovation, sustainability and inclusion. It uses SBERF and NFIB data plus examples of local ventures such as Second Chance Chic, Delia's Kitchen and Sky Limit Drones. It closes by calling for supportive public policy and continued local patronage.
one_line: Small businesses boost community development through jobs, local money circulation, innovation, sustainability and inclusion, supported by SBERF and NFIB data and local examples.
key_facts: An SBERF study released October 14, 2023 defines small businesses as entities with fewer than 500 employees and says they make up 99.9% of US businesses.
Emily Rodriguez launched the boutique thrift store 'Second Chance Chic' in Dayton, Ohio, in spring 2024; it revitalized a dilapidated storefront and employs six people.
Delia's Kitchen is a family-owned diner in South Chicago, owned by Delia Smith and dating back to September 2023, which hosts charity breakfasts with proceeds going to local schools and hospitals.
Delia Smith says: "It's all about giving back to the community that raised you."
Michael Thomson opened the coworking space 'Crafty Minds' in December 2024 and invites local business owners to mentor budding entrepreneurs in workshops.
SBERF's study estimates that for every dollar spent at a small business, approximately 67 cents stay within the local community (the multiplier effect).
Seventeen-year-old Alex Garcia launched 'Sky Limit Drones', a drone photography business in Santa Barbara, California, on August 15, 2024.
Lila Madison, a horticulturist, started 'Green Roots Landscaping' in February 2025, offering eco-friendly landscaping with indigenous plants and sustainable practices.
An NFIB report published September 28, 2025 found that communities with many diverse small businesses had higher employment rates and more resilience against economic downturns.
NFIB findings also showed these neighborhoods had greater community engagement and stronger communal support systems than areas dominated by malls and big-box retailers.
Jamal Anderson and Aisha Liu founded 'The Coding Hive', an IT training center, on November 1, 2024 to help people gain marketable skills and narrow the employment gap.
The note says tax incentives, financial aid and educational resources from government and non-profits are increasingly imperative to support small businesses.
